messages.subject: Analysis of DIA (SWATH-MS) data processed by different software tools
parts:
Dear MsStats developers and users,

I am currently applying MsStats for the downstream analysis of SWATH-MS data from a AB Sciex tripleTOF 5600. Identification and quantification of chromatographic peaks is mostly done in skyline-daily. Afterwards I compute the MsStats input file (10 column format) by using the skyline-results grid with the custom MsStatsView. Here is the head of the corresponding data.frame in R:

The data comes from an dilution experiment with a label-free design. MsStats creates quantitative features from this input data by combining the PeptdieSequence_PrecursorCharge_FragmentIOn_ProdcutCharge. Each feature therefor represents one transition. Feature grouping is done using the ProteinName.

An alternative tool for identification and quantification of chromatographic peaks in DIA data is spectronaut by biognosys. In contrast to skyline, is does not report a quant. value for every transition, but a value that represents the complete transition group (all transitions originating from the same precursor). Biognosys calls transition group = fragment group (FG). Here is the head of a data.frame after importing spectronaut results:

My questions:

It is quit easy to re-format this data frame to a format that equals the 10 column format requested by MsStats, BUT I can not de-convolute the FG.TotalPeakArea or FG.TotalPeakHeight, meaning features will equal a transition group, not a single transition!

What are the consequences in terms of statistics analysis when running MSstats? To me the data structure now looks similar to a DDA MS1 level analysis. On the MSstats homepage you suggest to use label-free DDA for this (colums for fragment information get NAs). Am I getting this right?

messages.author: 701dadf5d5bd3f3b
messages.subject: Re: Analysis of DIA (SWATH-MS) data processed by different software tools
parts:
Dear Tobias,

You are doing this correctly. If the signal processing groups all the fragments, then the data structure is the same as in label-free DDA and technically it can be analyzed as such.

The real question is whether this is a good thing to do. On one hand, by combining multiple fragments into a single feature we lose information (e.g. if one of the fragments is poor quality, it affects the entire feature). On the other hand, if the combination of the fragments into a feature is done in an intelligent way (e.g. only keeping good-quality features, consistently keeping the same fragments across all the runs to avoid bias, and eliminating missing values) then this can potentially be a good thing. 

Of course the users may not have much choice in this, but it is possible to use multiple spectral processing tools and compare. Would it be possible for you to share with us your results, at least at a very high and non-detailed level? It will be interesting to know which approach was beneficial.

Best wishes
Olga Vitek
